scoreNote: Strong-adequate (4.5): grants that scrutiny damages reputations, then argues genuine heroes remain possible; two developed examples with analysis, controlled prose at about 400 words on a memorable First and Second skeleton.

sentences.text: In an age of cameras and constant news, the private lives of famous people are exposed as never before.
One claim holds that society can no longer regard any living person as a hero, on the reason that media scrutiny eventually diminishes anyone's reputation.
I agree that intense scrutiny can damage reputations, but I disagree that genuine heroes have therefore become impossible.

sections.role: Body 1 — The truth in the reason

sentences.text: First, there is real force in the reason offered for the claim.
Modern media examine every detail of a famous person's life, and almost no one looks perfect under such a harsh light.
For example, several admired leaders and athletes have seen their images badly damaged once their private faults became public.
This shows that constant scrutiny can indeed strip away the shine that heroes once enjoyed.
When we learn that a hero is flawed and ordinary, our admiration can cool surprisingly quickly.
The endless search for scandal can make lasting, untouched reputations much harder to maintain.
To this extent, the reason given for the claim is genuinely persuasive.

sections.role: Body 2 — Why heroes are still possible

sentences.text: Second, however, the claim that no living person can be a hero goes much too far.
A hero need not be perfect, but only admirable for genuine courage, kindness, or sacrifice.
Consider the doctors, rescue workers, and ordinary people who risk their lives for others and are rightly admired by all who hear of them.
Their example shows that scrutiny cannot erase real acts of courage and goodness.
Knowing that heroes have faults can even make them more believable and more inspiring, not less.
Many people today are still widely respected precisely because their good deeds survive close examination.
Real heroism, then, can endure scrutiny rather than being destroyed by it.
In conclusion, media scrutiny does expose the flaws that once stayed hidden in famous lives.
But this does not make heroes impossible, since true courage and goodness remain visible and admired.
We can still honour living heroes, as long as we expect them to be genuinely good rather than flawless.
